```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 120
)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
```

`spseg` is a package for calculating bespoke local environments and segregation measures in R. It is heavily inspired by the methodological innovations in segregation measurement that Sean Reardon, David O'Sullivan, Kendra Bischoff, and colleagues presented in a series of papers in the 2000s. The package synthesizes these methodological innovations into a coherent measurement framework supported by a `spseg_result` class and corresponding extraction methods. The heaviest computations use compiled C++ code, with Boost C++ libraries supporting bandwidth-based and k-nearest-neighbor searches in Euclidean spaces and on graphs.

This vignette provides an overview of key features of the spseg package, starting from a simulated data set featuring individuals characterized by a categorical group membership, an ordinal status, and a continuous covariate. Segregation measures are generated based on this individual-level data, which is an ideal case for segregation measurement. From there, the data are compiled into spatial aggregates and the continuous covariate is binned. The performance and features of the package are then demonstrated on these spatially aggregated statistics, illustrating the kinds of data that researchers are likely to encounter in their own applications.


# Simulating a segregated population

Before we get going, let's load the packages used in this vignette:

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(spseg)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
```

We start by generating 5,000 fictive housing units and 5,000 fictive actors, which are distributed in different patterns across four scenarios. The housing units are uniformly and randomly distributed locations within a square. The agents have a binary trait, `group`, an ordinal trait, `status`, and a continuous trait, `resources`. These could represent, for example, race/ethnicity, education, and income. These variables are related: members of group A tend to have higher statuses than members of group B. Those in group A and those with higher status also tend to have more resources. 

```{r agents}
set.seed(2026)
N <- 2000L
side <- 1000
resource_mean <- 10
resource_gini <- 0.5
resource_sd <- sqrt(2) * qnorm((1 + resource_gini) / 2)
resource_noise <- 1

resource_sample <- sort(rlnorm(
  N,
  log(resource_mean) - resource_sd^2 / 2,
  resource_sd
))

stdz <- function(x) {
  (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

locations <- tibble(
  point_id = seq_len(N),
  x = runif(N, 0, side),
  y = runif(N, 0, side)
)

agents <- tibble(
  agent_id = seq_len(N),
  group = sample(rep(c("A", "B"), each = N / 2))
) |>
  mutate(
    status = stdz(1L * (group == "A")) + resource_noise * rnorm(N),
    status = rank(status) / n(),
    status = case_when(
      status < (1 / 3) ~ 1L,
      status < (2 / 3) ~ 2L,
      .default = 3L
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    resources = stdz(status + 1L * (group == "A")) + resource_noise * rnorm(N),
    resources = resource_sample[rank(resources, ties = "first")],
    resources_rank = rank(resources),
    status = factor(status, levels = c(1, 2, 3), ordered = TRUE),
    group = factor(group)
  )
```

These agents are assigned to housing units based on a periodic (i.e., sinusoidal) function, the agent's resources, and random noise. Periodic functions and noise allow for different degrees of spatial clustering by income and group membership. Increasing `cycles` produces smaller clusters; increasing `noise` weakens sorting and makes a more even distribution. Only the agent-to-location assignment varies across scenarios. The number and placement of points and the covariate distributions for the agents are the same in each pattern.

```{r distribute-agents}
location_noise <- rnorm(N)
assign_city <- function(cycles = 1, noise = 0.5) {
  periodic <- with(
    locations,
    cos(2 * pi * cycles * x / side) *
      cos(2 * pi * cycles * y / side)
  )
  utility <- log((1 + 1e-6 + periodic) / 2)
  score <- as.numeric(scale(utility)) + noise * location_noise
  destination <- order(score, locations$point_id)
  source <- order(agents$resources, agents$agent_id)
  assigned <- integer(N)
  assigned[destination] <- source
  bind_cols(locations, slice(agents, assigned))
}

scenarios <- crossing(cycles = c(1, 3), noise = c(0, 1)) |>
  mutate(pattern = paste0(cycles, " cycle(s); noise = ", noise))

patterns <- map2(scenarios$cycles, scenarios$noise, assign_city) |>
  set_names(scenarios$pattern) |>
  imap(\(city, label) mutate(city, pattern = label))
```

We can visualize the distribution of resources and statuses across agents, and the spatial distribution of resources, statuses, and groups across the scenarios as follows:

```{r patterns, echo=FALSE}
agents |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = log(resources),
    y = after_stat(count),
    group = group,
    color = group,
    fill = group
  )) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(status), labeller = label_both, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Agents")

patterns |>
  bind_rows() |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = resources_rank)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "resource") +
  labs(title = "Resources") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()

colors <- viridis::mako(4)
patterns |>
  bind_rows() |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = status)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, ncol = 2) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_discrete(palette = colors, name = "status") +
  labs(title = "Status") +
  theme_void()

colors <- viridis::rocket(2)
patterns |>
  bind_rows() |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, ncol = 2) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Groups") +
  scale_color_discrete(palette = c("blue", "red"))
```


# Measuring segregation in individual data

We can calculate spatial segregation measures using the `spseg` function, here using the micro-data directly. The call below requests a k-nearest neighbors ("knn") approach applied to the first residential pattern using multiple different bandwidths. We can request the measures for multiple variables in one call using a list that nests calls to `spseg_categorical()`, `spseg_ordinal()`, and `spseg_continuous()` helper functions. This is computationally more efficient than calling the function separately for each variable (set), because we can reuse the same nearest neighbor calculations across variables. 

```{r micro-indices}
micro_variables <- list(
  group = spseg_categorical(vars = "group"),
  resources = spseg_continuous(
    vars = "resources",
    summary = list(type = "shares", probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
  ),
  status = spseg_ordinal(vars = "status")
)
bands <- c(25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 1000, 2000)
result <- spseg(
  patterns[[1]],
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  variables = micro_variables,
  bands = bands,
  neighbors = "knn",
  measures = "all",
  weighting = "biweight",
  scope = "both",
  output = "full"
)
```

Note that for continuous variables, we can specify a `summary` option. This influences how local environments and exposure measures are reported back, but doesn't influence the calculation of other segregation measures.

The output of the function, stored in `result`, has a package-specific `spseg_result` class with a set of names and methods. We can use `as.data.frame()` to extract different pieces of information from `result`. For example, the following extracts the overall segregation statistics and displays a slice of the resulting table:

```{r segstats-result}
result_overall <- result |>
  as.data.frame(what = "indices")

result_overall |>
  filter(band == 100) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

We can plot the overall segregation measures across all bands, producing the segregation curves described by Reardon and colleagues. The levels and rates of change change across bands are indicative of a combination of evenness and clustering forms of segregation. If one curves dominates another, the tells use that one pattern is more segregated, in terms of evenness, than the other. The rate of change of segregation across bands tells about the extent of clustering segregation: a faster rate of change indicates that clusters of particular groups or incomes are smaller, that population composition varies more over smaller distances, and that the pattern is more checkerboard like.

```{r single-pattern-curves, fig.height=6}
result_overall |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, color = measure)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable)) +
  labs(x = "Neighborhood population (kNN)", y = "Segregation index") +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1)
  )
```


We can also recover pairwise indices. When there are only two groups, these are the same as those presented above. But when there are multiple groups, as is the case with status and resources, then there multiple comparisons to be made:

```{r pairwise-result}
result_pairwise <- result |>
  as.data.frame(what = "pairwise") |>
  as_tibble()

result_pairwise |>
  filter(variable == 'status') |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

We can likewise plot the pairwise indices. These are all group-to-group binary indices. In the case of continuous variables, these are based on the `probs` argument, which featured quartile-based cutoffs. Below I filter down to dissimilarity indices and the resource variable only and plot these for the different pairs.

```{r pairwise-result}
result_pairwise |>
  filter(measure == 'information' & variable == 'resource') |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, color = group_b)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(group_a)) +
  labs(x = "Neighborhood population (kNN)", y = "Segregation index") +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1)
  )
```


The indices describe different aspects of segregation, so it is useful to look at
how each changes as we enlarge the neighborhood. The bandwidths here are numbers
of people before distance weighting, including the focal person; they are not
physical distances. The same kNN population can occupy a small radius in a dense
area and a larger radius elsewhere.

The categorical, ordinal, and continuous statistics have different definitions.
Compare scales within a variable and measure rather than treating the vertical
positions of different panels as directly comparable. Pairwise results, in turn,
compare two groups at a time. For resources, these are binary comparisons of the
specified income groups, not the full-resolution continuous index.

```{r single-pattern-pairwise}
result_pairwise |>
  filter(variable == "group", band == 100) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

# Obtaining local environments

We can also retrieve individualized neighborhood statistics because we requested the `"full"` output. That is we can characterize the local environment at various different values of bandwidth or k-nearest neighbors. If we apply `st_as_sf()`, we can get the local environments for the selected variables and bandwidths in a long spatial data frame. Here we continue with the first pattern, rather than combining patterns just yet.

```{r local-environments}
localenvs <- result |>
  st_as_sf(bands = c(100, 500))

localenvs |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(location, variable, band, category, value) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

We can extract and plot spatially weighted group shares from the local environment objects. We just need to pick the right variable and category. Here I align the color coding for the group shares with the color coding for plotting the raw data. The one change is that we now have continuous shares, rather than a binary variable, and the midpoint is colored white. This represents not the absence of population, but just equal (spatially weighted) representation:

```{r group-local-environments}
localenvs |>
  filter(variable == "group", category == "A") |>
  ggplot(aes(colour = value)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low = "#b2182b",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2166ac",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Local share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

For resources we requested shares in global quartile groups. The map below shows
the share of each person's neighborhood in the lowest resource quartile. It does
not show the neighborhood's median income or median global rank. To obtain local
rank quantiles instead, use `summary = list(type = "quantiles")`; these are a
different description of the same underlying neighborhood distribution.

```{r resource-local-environments}
resource_groups <- result$analyses$resources$definition$summary$groups$labels

localenvs |>
  filter(variable == "resources", category == resource_groups[[1]]) |>
  ggplot(aes(colour = value)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), name = "Local share Q1") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

## Exposure

Exposure averages these local shares among members of each focal group. Each row
of a share exposure matrix sums to one, and the diagonal is isolation. For
resources, the focal and target groups use the same quartiles we used for the
local environments. The continuous scalar indices still use the exact resource
values, rather than reducing everyone to quartile membership.

```{r single-pattern-exposure}
exposures <- result |>
  as.data.frame(what = "exposure") |>
  as_tibble()

exposures |>
  filter(variable == "group", band == 100) |>
  select(from_group, to_group, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = to_group, values_from = value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r resource-exposure}
exposures |>
  filter(variable == "resources", band %in% c(100, 500)) |>
  mutate(
    from_group = factor(
      from_group,
      levels = resource_groups,
      labels = paste0("Q", 1:4)
    ),
    to_group = factor(
      to_group,
      levels = resource_groups,
      labels = paste0("Q", 1:4)
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(to_group, from_group, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Neighbor's resource quartile", y = "Focal resource quartile")
```

Use the default `output = "indices"` when only indices and exposures are needed.
`output = "full"` additionally retains local environments and geometry;
`output = "localenv"` calculates local environments without indices or exposures.
Extract only the variables and bands you need when mapping large results.

# Aggregating the same people

We next replace the first pattern of individuals with a table of counts for 45
Voronoi polygons centered on randomly drawn points. The partition is generated
independently of the actors' attributes and clipped to our square. Resources are
divided into ten equal-population bins before aggregation, while group and status retain their
original categories. This resembles a small-area table containing marginal
counts for several population characteristics.

```{r voronoi-partition}
people <- patterns[[1]] |>
  mutate(resources_bin = cut_number(resources, n = 10)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), remove = FALSE)

domain <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(
  xmin = 0,
  ymin = 0,
  xmax = side,
  ymax = side
)))

set.seed(2027)
seed_points <- tibble(
  x = runif(45, 0, side),
  y = runif(45, 0, side)
) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"))

voronoi_geometry <- seed_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = domain) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_intersection(domain)

voronoi <- st_sf(
  zone_id = seq_along(voronoi_geometry),
  geometry = voronoi_geometry
)
```

These are synthetic planar coordinates, so no real-world CRS is assigned. For
actual geographic data, use an appropriate projected CRS before constructing
polygons or calculating Euclidean distance bands.

The following pipeline joins people to polygons, counts their categories, and
pivots the counts into one row per polygon. `complete()` retains empty zones and
categories. Separate marginal tables are sufficient for these three analyses;
we are not asking for segregation of their joint combinations.

```{r aggregate-counts}
group_columns <- paste0("group_", levels(agents$group))
status_columns <- paste0("status_", levels(agents$status))
income_columns <- sprintf("income_%02d", 1:10)
count_columns <- c(group_columns, status_columns, income_columns)

membership <- st_within(people, voronoi)
stopifnot(all(lengths(membership) == 1L))

zone_counts <- people |>
  st_join(voronoi, join = st_within) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  transmute(
    zone_id,
    group = as.character(group),
    status = as.character(status),
    income = sprintf("%02d", as.integer(resources_bin))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-zone_id, names_to = "variable", values_to = "category") |>
  count(zone_id, variable, category, name = "population") |>
  unite("category", variable, category) |>
  complete(
    zone_id = voronoi$zone_id,
    category = count_columns,
    fill = list(population = 0L)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = population)

voronoi_counts <- voronoi |>
  left_join(zone_counts, by = "zone_id")

# Each trait must still account for all of the original people.
stopifnot(
  sum(select(zone_counts, all_of(group_columns)) |> as.matrix()) == N,
  sum(select(zone_counts, all_of(status_columns)) |> as.matrix()) == N,
  sum(select(zone_counts, all_of(income_columns)) |> as.matrix()) == N
)

voronoi_counts |>
  mutate(share_A = group_A / (group_A + group_B)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = share_A), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = seed_points, size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#b2182b",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2166ac",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Zone share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

Column order gives the order of status categories and income intervals. For
income, `representation = "intervals"` uses a linearly interpolated rank CDF,
rather than substituting bin midpoints. The bins no longer supply anyone's exact
income. Requested quartile groups can split these decile intervals, so the package
warns about proportional allocation within intervals. The same allocation is used
for focal population and neighbor shares. This assumes the same within-interval
rank distribution at every location; it does not recover sorting hidden by bins.

```{r count-specifications}
count_variables <- list(
  group = spseg_categorical(vars = group_columns),
  resources = spseg_continuous(
    vars = income_columns,
    representation = "intervals",
    summary = list(type = "shares", probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
  ),
  status = spseg_ordinal(vars = status_columns)
)
```

## Non-spatial measures on the polygons

To treat polygons as mutually exclusive units, set `bands = 0` with raw support
and unweighted neighborhoods. Each polygon's local environment then contains
only its own population, because these polygons have distinct centroids. Polygon
adjacency and distance between polygons play no role in this calculation. This
is not the same as running `bands = 0` on individual points, where each distinct
location would contain just its own resident.

```{r aggregate-nonspatial}
nonspatial <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  neighbors = "radius",
  bands = 0,
  weighting = "unweighted",
  surface = "raw",
  scope = "overall",
  output = "full"
)

nonspatial |>
  as.data.frame(what = "indices") |>
  select(variable, measure, value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

We can check the own-polygon interpretation directly. The local share of group A
must equal its observed share in that polygon.

```{r own-polygon-check}
observed_shares <- zone_counts |>
  arrange(zone_id) |>
  mutate(share_A = group_A / (group_A + group_B)) |>
  pull(share_A)

calculated_shares <- nonspatial |>
  as.data.frame(what = "env", variables = "group") |>
  filter(category == "group_A") |>
  arrange(location) |>
  pull(value)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(calculated_shares, observed_shares)))
```

## Spatial measures on the polygons

For spatial calculations, we first use the raw polygon support with distance
bands. The default raw representation puts all of a polygon's counts at its
centroid. A neighborhood includes the focal polygon and nearby centroids, with
biweight distance weights. It does not select parts of polygons intersected by
a circular buffer. Distances here are in our synthetic coordinate units.

```{r aggregate-spatial}
radius_bands <- c(25, 50, 75, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500)

centroid_spatial <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  neighbors = "radius",
  bands = radius_bands,
  weighting = "biweight",
  surface = "raw",
  scope = "overall"
)
```

Alternatively, `surface = "grid"` spreads each polygon's population uniformly
among fine-grid cells assigned to it before measuring spatial neighborhoods.
The next call uses a 30 by 30 grid. This changes the assumed within-polygon
population surface, while retaining source counts when each polygon contains
cell centers. It does not reconstruct the original point pattern.

```{r aggregate-grid}
uniform_spatial <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  neighbors = "radius",
  bands = radius_bands,
  weighting = "biweight",
  surface = "grid",
  nrow = 30,
  ncol = 30,
  scope = "overall"
)

uniform_spatial$surface_info$fallback
```

The fallback record identifies source polygons without fine-grid cell centers;
use a finer grid if this occurs. For pycnophylactic smoothing and source-zone
count audits, see the [surface guide](spseg-surface-construction.html).

```{r aggregate-comparison}
aggregate_curves <- list(
  "Polygon centroids" = centroid_spatial,
  "Uniform population grid" = uniform_spatial
) |>
  map(as.data.frame) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "support")

nonspatial_indices <- nonspatial |>
  as.data.frame(what = "indices") |>
  filter(measure == "information")

aggregate_curves |>
  filter(measure == "information") |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = support)) +
  geom_hline(
    data = nonspatial_indices,
    aes(yintercept = value),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood radius (coordinate units)",
    y = "Information index",
    colour = "Population support"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The dashed lines show the non-spatial polygon indices. Changes in zoning, income
binning, surface resolution, and spatial weighting can all change the results;
there is no requirement that every transformation move the index in the same
direction. These radius profiles also use different neighborhoods from the
population kNN profiles in the first part of the vignette.

# Running all patterns in parallel

We now return to the original microdata and analyze all four patterns. This time
we use the distance bands above, rather than population kNN. All patterns retain
the same locations and trait distributions, making the comparison about their
spatial arrangement. Variables within a pattern still share one neighbor search;
separate patterns are independent jobs that we can run in parallel.

The helper below uses two PSOCK workers from R's `parallel` package, which is
included with R and works on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Each worker runs a
separate R process and loads the installed spseg package using the parent
session's library paths. Install the current package before running this example.
The helper stops the
workers when it finishes, including if a calculation raises an error. Use fewer
workers when memory is limited; starting workers can cost more than it saves for
small examples. No random numbers are drawn in these calls: the simulated
patterns have already been generated with fixed seeds.

```{r parallel-patterns}
run_patterns <- function(patterns, variables, bands, workers = 2L) {
  cluster <- parallel::makePSOCKcluster(workers)
  on.exit(parallel::stopCluster(cluster), add = TRUE)
  parallel::clusterCall(cluster, function(paths) .libPaths(paths), .libPaths())

  parallel::parLapply(
    cluster,
    patterns,
    function(city, variables, bands) {
      spseg::spseg(
        city,
        coords = c("x", "y"),
        variables = variables,
        bands = bands,
        neighbors = "radius",
        weighting = "biweight",
        measures = "all",
        scope = "both",
        output = "full"
      )
    },
    variables = variables,
    bands = bands
  )
}

pattern_results <- run_patterns(patterns, micro_variables, radius_bands)
```

The parallel call returns a named list in the same order as `patterns`. For a
sequential run, the equivalent tidyverse call is:

```{r sequential-patterns, eval=FALSE}
pattern_results <- patterns |>
  map(\(city) {
    spseg(
      city,
      coords = c("x", "y"),
      variables = micro_variables,
      bands = radius_bands,
      neighbors = "radius",
      weighting = "biweight",
      measures = "all",
      scope = "both",
      output = "full"
    )
  })
```

`output = "full"` is useful here because we will map selected environments.
For many large patterns, return only indices when possible and extract selected
local summaries inside the worker to limit memory use and data transfer.

# Comparing patterns

We can compile the segregation measures into a data frame while preserving the
pattern names, then join the simulation settings. This avoids relying on list
positions or relabeling factors after combining the results.

```{r pattern-indices}
curves <- pattern_results |>
  map(as.data.frame) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "pattern") |>
  left_join(scenarios, by = "pattern")

curves |>
  filter(band == 100, measure == "information") |>
  select(pattern, variable, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Now we can plot segregation curves for each measure and variable. Colors identify
the same pattern across panels. We compare patterns within each panel; the
categorical, ordinal, and continuous measures are not interchangeable.

```{r pattern-curves, fig.height=7}
curves |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(variable ~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood radius (coordinate units)",
    y = "Segregation index",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

## Local environments across patterns

To make thumbnails of local environments, extract only the group and radii we
want to compare before combining results. Keep a common color scale across
panels; otherwise similar colors could represent different local compositions.

```{r pattern-local-environments, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
pattern_local <- pattern_results |>
  map(\(x) {
    st_as_sf(x, variables = "group", bands = c(100, 300)) |>
      filter(category == "A")
  }) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "pattern") |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  mutate(pattern = factor(pattern, levels = names(patterns)))

pattern_local |>
  ggplot(aes(colour = value)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(band), cols = vars(pattern)) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low = "#b2182b",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#2166ac",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Local share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Exposures across patterns

Finally, we can compare how exposure changes with neighborhood radius. The
following curves show exposure to group A separately for focal groups A and B.
For focal group A, this is isolation; for focal group B, it is exposure to A.
Both panels use a common zero-to-one scale.

```{r pattern-exposures}
pattern_exposure <- pattern_results |>
  map(\(x) as.data.frame(x, what = "exposure", variables = "group")) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "pattern")

pattern_exposure |>
  filter(to_group == "A") |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~from_group, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood radius (coordinate units)",
    y = "Exposure to A",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

The [multiple-variable guide](spseg-multiple-variables.html) gives measurement
definitions and sources. The [surface guide](spseg-surface-construction.html)
examines allocation, smoothing, and conservation. For supplied adjacency or road
networks, see [network segregation](spseg-networks.html).
